Ditch
dich
n. (rendering Hebrew shachath/gēb, Greek bothunos)
From Saxon dic, a trench or dike — the same word gives both ditch, the hollow dug, and dike, the bank thrown up beside it. In Scripture the ditch is usually a pit: something a man digs, and something a man falls into, and the two are often the same man.

Biblical Definition

The ditch in Scripture is a trap, and it is remarkable how often the digger is the victim. David states it as a settled providence: “He made a pit, and digged it, and is fallen into the ditch which he made” (Psalm 7:15) — not an accident but a moral order, in which mischief returns upon the head that devised it. Job uses the word for the utter defilement of a man before a holy God, and the honesty of it is bracing: even if he washed himself with snow water, “yet shalt thou plunge me in the ditch, and mine own clothes shall abhor me” (Job 9:31) — self-cleansing cannot survive contact with God's holiness. The Lord Jesus makes the ditch the destination of a whole method of religion: “they be blind leaders of the blind. And if the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch” (Matthew 15:14) — teacher and taught in the same hole, which is the most sobering thing ever said about false teaching. And once, memorably, God commands ditches be dug as an act of faith before there is any sign of water: “Thus saith the LORD, Make this valley full of ditches” (2 Kings 3:16), and the water came without wind or rain. The ditch a man digs for his brother takes him; the ditch a man digs at God's word is filled.

Webster 1828 Definition

A trench in the earth made by digging; a pit or hollow. In Scripture, the ditch a man digs and falls into himself, the ditch of defilement in Job, the ditch into which the blind leading the blind must fall, and the ditches dug at the LORD's command and filled without rain.

expand to see more

DITCH, n. 1. A trench in the earth made by digging, particularly a trench for draining wet land, or for making a fence.

2. Any long hollow receptacle of water.

3. A pit or hole into which one may fall.

4. From Saxon dic, a ditch or dike; the same word as dike, the bank thrown up from the trench.

5. In Scripture, is fallen into the ditch which he made, Ps. 7; both shall fall into the ditch, Matt. 15.

Key Scripture

Psalm 7:15 — "He made a pit, and digged it, and is fallen into the ditch which he made."

Job 9:31 — "Yet shalt thou plunge me in the ditch, and mine own clothes shall abhor me."

Matthew 15:14 — "Let them alone: they be blind leaders of the blind. And if the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch."

2 Kings 3:16 — "And he said, Thus saith the LORD, Make this valley full of ditches."

Modern Corruption

False teaching is treated as a private mistake affecting only the teacher, when Scripture says the blind guide takes his hearers into the pit with him; and the digging of ditches by God's word is replaced by strategies that require no faith at all.

expand to see more

Matthew 15:14 is the reason the New Testament is so severe about teachers. Error is not contained in the man who holds it; it travels down every rank that trusts him, and the Lord's picture has the guide and the guided ending in the same ditch. James warns that teachers receive the greater condemnation; Paul tells Timothy to take heed unto himself and unto the doctrine, for in so doing he shall both save himself and them that hear him. The modern reluctance to name false teachers — on the grounds that it is unkind, divisive, or above our pay grade — is measured against a Lord who called the leading religious authorities of His day blind guides to their faces, and told His disciples plainly to let them alone. Charity toward persons is not owed to their doctrine.

The second use of the ditch is a rebuke to a different kind of blindness. Elisha told three kings to dig ditches in a dry valley with no cloud in the sky, and the digging was the whole of their part; God supplied the water. Faith of that shape is rare because it looks foolish until it is vindicated, and church planning increasingly prefers methods that will work whether or not God moves. There is no virtue in digging ditches nobody was told to dig, and Scripture nowhere commends recklessness. But where God has given a word — preach, pray, gather, disciple, endure — obedience is to dig, in dry ground, before the water comes. The valley filled without wind and without rain, and every man who had refused to dig had a trench-shaped share of nothing.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shachath, a pit or corruption; gēb, a cistern or trench; Greek bothunos, a pit or hole in the ground.

expand to see more

Hebrew shachath (H7845) — a pit, ditch, or destruction; “fallen into the ditch which he made” (Psalm 7:15).

Hebrew gēb (H1356) — a pit, trench, or cistern; the ditches Elisha commanded in the valley (2 Kings 3:16).

Hebrew shuchah (H7745) — a pit dug as a trap; “a strange woman is a narrow pit” (Proverbs 23:27).

Greek bothunos (G999) — a pit or ditch; the hole into which the blind guide and his followers fall (Matthew 15:14).

Greek hodēgos — a guide or leader; the word behind “blind leaders,” properly one who shows the way.

Usage

"Of mischief returning on its author: He made a pit, and digged it, and is fallen into the ditch which he made (Psalm 7:15)."

"Of teacher and taught sharing one end: if the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch (Matthew 15:14)."

"Of obedience before provision: Thus saith the LORD, Make this valley full of ditches (2 Kings 3:16)."
